subtopics.title: From Self-Sufficiency to Surplus and Barter

questions.question: The trap inside self-sufficiency was that:
options: A household consumes only what its own hands produce — every craft practised badly under every roof, no skill pursued to excellence

questions.question: Surplus is the pivot of economic history because:
options: It frees hands from food production — specialists emerge, and a specialist must EXCHANGE what they make
It belonged to the ruler alone

questions.question: The DOUBLE COINCIDENCE OF WANTS requires:
options: A partner who both HAS what you seek and WANTS what you carry — a search costly enough to throttle exchange

questions.question: Barter's four defects are:
options: Double coincidence of wants; indivisibility; no common measure of value; no store of value

subtopics.title: Money and the Evolution of Markets

questions.question: Money's defining functions are:
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value — with divisibility fitting any purchase size

questions.question: Commodity moneys that survived — cattle, salt, shells, metals — shared the properties of being:
options: Durable, divisible, portable and scarce — with precious metals scoring highest on all four

questions.question: Mercantile and commercial law arose because:
options: Kings wished to slow trade down
Strangers cannot trade on kinship and memory — contracts, standard weights and courts turned personal trust into institutional trust

questions.question: The company, with ownership sliced into shares, evolved because:
options: Rulers required it for all trade
Risk could be spread across many holders and capital assembled at sums no single merchant could risk alone

questions.question: The state's three great entries into the market were:
options: Involvement in trade, taxation, and financing infrastructure

questions.question: Taxation rewired the ruler's incentives because:
options: More economic activity means more revenue — the ruler gained a permanent interest in growth, and the taxed in how revenue is spent

questions.question: Infrastructure is the textbook case for public investment because it:
options: Costs enormously, benefits everybody, and repays its builder only indirectly — so no individual trader will build it

questions.question: The analytical thread through all three entries is that:
options: Each entry answers a LIMITATION of the market — the intervention logic of term two, wearing historical dress

questions.question: Industrialisation's four components are:
options: Manufacturing, technological progress, mobilisation of energy, mechanisation

questions.question: The mobilisation of energy was the true rupture because:
options: Work had always been limited by muscle — water, steam, electricity and oil drove production past every limit a living body imposes
Energy replaced the need for money

questions.question: Alongside its gains, industrialisation's bill included:
options: Brutal factory conditions, children at machines, and fouled air and water — the abuses that called labour law and regulation into existence

questions.question: South Africa entered the industrial age through:
options: MINING — diamonds then gold, railways flung inland, and labour concentrated under the migrant labour system whose social costs the country still carries

subtopics.title: The Village That Fed Itself — Then Grew Extra

questions.question: No family in the river valley traded because:
options: No family ever had anything LEFT OVER — and doing every job meant doing no job well

questions.question: The farmer's extra millet mattered because:
options: It could be thrown to the fish
It released other hands from the fields — her brother becomes the full-time ironworker, the neighbour the weaver, the boy the fisherman
It raised the price of grain

questions.question: The four miseries of swapping were:
options: Long roads, heavy loads, slow boats, high tolls
The hunt for the exact partner; big goods for small purchases; every deal an argument without a yardstick; wealth that rots or wanders off

questions.question: "Money is half a trade you can keep in your pocket" means:
options: The two halves of every swap were sliced apart — sell to anyone now, hold the copper, buy from anyone later
Money buys only half of anything
Half the village must accept it

questions.question: The village's four requirements for its money were:
options: Lasting, splittable, scarce, carryable — a test passed by cattle, salt, shells, gold, notes and the balance on a banking app alike

questions.question: When strangers began trading with strangers, the village needed:
options: RULES — stamped weights, kept promises, an elder to judge disputes: trust moving from family knowledge into institutions

questions.question: Twenty families each buying a SHARE of a trading expedition meant:
options: The chief took all the profits
Only one family bore the risk
Profits were divided and no single family was destroyed if the boat was lost — risk spread, capital gathered

subtopics.title: The Chief, and Then the Machines

questions.question: The chief's three moves — still in every national budget — are:
options: REGULATE the trade, TAX the granaries and deals, BUILD what no trader would build alone

questions.question: After he began taxing, the chief wanted the market to THRIVE because:
options: A busier market filled his stores faster — the ruler became the economy's interested party

questions.question: Across the mill floor, the two new kinds of people were:
options: The family that OWNS the mill and the hundreds who WORK in it — whose quarrels become labour relations

questions.question: The valley's full journey, in proper order:
options: Extra → specialists → copper → market (roads, rules, shares) → chief → machines
